%=================================================================
% Abstract (<= ~200 words, one paragraph: background, methods, results, conclusion)
% All numbers: docs/publication/STAGE_C_MODES_RESULTS.md (2026-11-05).
\abstract{Research gaps stated by authors could feed automated idea generation, but they are rare and scattered in papers. Asking a large language model (LLM) to judge every sentence, or a whole paper at once, is expensive, and long inputs are hard for smaller models. We propose a hierarchical three-stage funnel that splits the task: rules drop unlikely text, a zero-shot natural-language-inference classifier flags candidate gaps, and an LLM filters the candidates as source sentences. A single instruction sets the filter to favour precision, balance or recall. We evaluated the funnel on two human-labelled benchmarks, SAL (limitations in randomized-trial reports) and FWS (future work in natural language processing papers). Because each labels only one gap type in one field, we also built a corpus of 230 arXiv and biomedical papers in which two LLMs labelled limitations, future work and research gaps, with a third LLM pass resolving disagreements, and evaluated on it as well. In its high-precision setting, the filter raised precision on SAL from 29.1\% to 66.2\% at 84.9\% recall, reached $F_1$ 0.760 on FWS, and reached 86.6\% precision at 57.4\% recall on this corpus. On every dataset the three settings traded precision for recall as intended. The training-free classifier nearly matched a supervised PubMedBERT in $F_1$ ($-$0.021) but was 8.4 points less precise. The funnel needed 3.7--13 times fewer LLM input tokens than judging every sentence, but only 1.25--3.1 times fewer than whole-paper calls. We also show that letter case reveals the label in FWS.}

% Keywords (3--10, semicolon-separated)
\keyword{research gap extraction; limitations; future work; scientific text mining; large language models; natural language inference; zero-shot classification; LLM filtering}
